metadata.title: EAU GUIDELINES ON NON-NEUROGENIC FEMALE LUTS
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the assessment and management of non-neurogenic lower urinary tract symptoms in women, extending its scope beyond urinary incontinence to other functional urological conditions. It covers overactive bladder, forms of urinary incontinence, underactive bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, nocturia, pelvic organ prolapse with LUTS, urinary fistula and urethral diverticulum. The document provides diagnostic, conservative, pharmacological, procedural and surgical recommendations, along with treatment-related follow-up.

conditions_covered: non-neurogenic female lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
care_settings: Centres with appropriate experience for complicated stress urinary incontinence
target_population: Adults with overactive bladder or urinary incontinence

toxicities.event: Dry mouth
toxicities.incidence: Anticholinergic drugs cause more adverse events than placebo. Dry mouth occurs less often with transdermal oxybutynin than with oral anticholinergic drugs, and less often with beta-3 agonists than with antimuscarinics.
prevention: When anticholinergic treatment is appropriate, consider an extended-release formulation where possible; once-daily extended-release formulations have fewer adverse events than immediate-release preparations.
Review efficacy and adverse effects early after starting anticholinergic medication.

toxicities.event: Cognitive impairment associated with anticholinergic treatment
toxicities.incidence: Anticholinergic drugs cause more adverse events than placebo.
prevention: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously in elderly women, particularly those with cognitive dysfunction or a risk of developing it.
Assess anticholinergic burden and associated comorbidities when considering anticholinergic therapy for overactive bladder syndrome.

toxicities.event: Constipation associated with anticholinergic treatment
toxicities.incidence: Anticholinergic drugs cause more adverse events than placebo.
prevention: Review adverse effects early in patients taking anticholinergic medication for overactive bladder.

toxicities.event: Skin reactions
toxicities.incidence: Skin reactions lead to a high rate of treatment withdrawal.

toxicities.event: Gastrointestinal and central nervous system adverse effects
toxicities.incidence: These effects may be significant and result in a high rate of discontinuation; they may be confined to the first weeks of treatment.
prevention: Counsel selected patients about adverse-event risks before offering duloxetine.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Start and withdraw duloxetine through dose titration because of its high adverse-event risk.

toxicities.event: Hyponatraemia
recognition: Serum sodium concentration below the normal range
prevention: Counsel women about hyponatraemia and other risks before desmopressin treatment for nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria.
Carefully monitor serum sodium concentration in elderly patients receiving desmopressin.
Avoid prescribing desmopressin when baseline serum sodium concentration is below the normal range.

toxicities.event: Voiding dysfunction and increased post-void residual volume
toxicities.incidence: Voiding dysfunction occurs more often with onabotulinumtoxinA than with antimuscarinics.
recognition: Possible prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation
prevention: Before offering onabotulinumtoxinA, explain the possibility of a prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

toxicities.event: Urinary tract infection after bladder wall injection
prevention: Explain the urinary tract infection risk before offering onabotulinumtoxinA.

toxicities.event: Bacteriuria after bladder wall injection
toxicities.incidence: The risk after onabotA (100 U) injection is high, but its clinical significance remains uncertain.

toxicities.event: Implant lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear
prevention: Provide life-long surveillance to women with a sacral nerve stimulation implant to monitor for these problems.

toxicities.event: Need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation after augmentation cystoplasty
prevention: Before augmentation cystoplasty, explain this risk and establish that the patient is willing and able to perform clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

toxicities.event: Malignancy after augmentation cystoplasty
prevention: Provide life-long surveillance after augmentation cystoplasty, including cystoscopic surveillance because of the malignancy risk.

toxicities.event: Voiding dysfunction and postoperative urinary tract infection after autologous sling placement
toxicities.incidence: Both occur more often after autologous sling placement than after open colposuspension, although the overall adverse-event rates are similar.
prevention: Discuss the risks and benefits relative to other surgical approaches before offering autologous sling placement.

toxicities.event: Pelvic organ prolapse and bladder or urethral perforation after autologous sling placement
toxicities.incidence: These events occur less often after autologous sling placement than after open colposuspension.

toxicities.event: Bladder perforation and voiding dysfunction with retropubic sling insertion
toxicities.incidence: Compared with the transobturator route, retropubic insertion has a higher intraoperative bladder-perforation risk and a higher voiding-dysfunction rate. The top-to-bottom (inside-out) retropubic direction is associated with a higher risk of postoperative voiding dysfunction.
prevention: Explain complications associated with MUS procedures and discuss alternative treatments.

toxicities.event: Groin pain with transobturator sling insertion
toxicities.incidence: The risk is higher with transobturator than with retropubic insertion.
prevention: Discuss the risks and benefits of MUS routes with women considering surgery.

toxicities.event: Mesh exposure, repeat stress urinary incontinence surgery and dyspareunia after single-incision slings
toxicities.incidence: At three years, these outcomes occur more often with single-incision slings (Ajust® and Altis®) than with conventional MUS.
recognition: Need for repeat stress urinary incontinence surgery
prevention: Explain MUS complications and alternative treatments to women considering these procedures.
Tell women offered a single-incision sling that its long-term efficacy remains uncertain.

toxicities.event: Adverse events associated with urethral bulking agents
toxicities.incidence: Autologous fat and hyaluronic acid have a higher adverse-event risk. Overall adverse-event rates with urethral bulking agents are lower than with open surgery.
prevention: Do not offer autologous fat or hyaluronic acid as urethral bulking agents because of their higher adverse-event risk.

toxicities.event: Urinary retention after urethral bulking injection
toxicities.incidence: Periurethral injection may carry a higher urinary-retention risk than transurethral injection.

toxicities.event: Complications, mechanical failure and need for explantation
toxicities.incidence: The risk is high, even in expert centres.
prevention: Explain these risks to women considering an artificial urinary sphincter or adjustable compression device.

toxicities.event: Postoperative stress urinary incontinence, vesicovaginal fistula and urethral stricture
prevention: Advise women undergoing bladder neck incision about these possible postoperative outcomes.

toxicities.event: Postoperative urinary incontinence after internal urethrotomy
prevention: When offering internal urethrotomy for bladder outlet obstruction due to urethral stricture disease, explain the urinary incontinence risk and the limited long-term improvement.

toxicities.event: Recurrent stress urinary incontinence after sling revision
prevention: Explain the risk of recurrent SUI and the possible need for repeat or concurrent anti-UI surgery before sling revision.

toxicities.event: Pelvic organ prolapse associated with abdominal straining
prevention: Warn women with underactive bladder (UAB) who strain abdominally to empty their bladder about the POP risk.

toxicities.event: Cancer developing within a urethral diverticulum
toxicities.incidence: The risk during conservative treatment is small (1–6%).
prevention: If conservative treatment is chosen, inform patients of the risk of cancer developing within the diverticulum.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Offer prophylactic antibiotics only after discussing the risk of increasing antimicrobial resistance.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with recurrent urinary tract infections

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not routinely use ureteric stents to prevent injury during routine gynaecological surgery.

infection_management.prevention: Before bladder wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA, inform patients about the urinary tract infection risk.
infection_management.management: If urinary tract infection is present, reassess LUTS after its treatment.

infection_management.prevention: Offer prophylactic antibiotics only after discussing the risk of increasing antimicrobial resistance.

infection_management.management: Do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly patients for the purpose of improving urinary incontinence.
Individualise the timing of fistula repair and proceed once infection, along with any oedema, inflammation or tissue necrosis, has resolved.

conditions.name: nonneurogenic female lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
conditions.description: The guideline covers storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms in women, including functional conditions that need not involve urinary incontinence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms may involve urine storage, voiding or the period after micturition. Assessment also considers sexual, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms, urgency episodes, and the type, timing and severity of urinary incontinence.

conditions.name: Overactive bladder
conditions.description: A symptom complex centred on urinary urgency, commonly accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency-related incontinence, when urinary tract infection or another evident disorder is absent.
conditions.epidemiology: Obesity is a risk factor for urinary incontinence in women, although its relationship with other OAB symptoms is uncertain.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urgency may occur with frequency, nocturia and urge urinary incontinence. In older people, LUTS are associated with cardiac failure, chronic renal failure, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, neurological disease, general cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, depression and metabolic syndrome.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up depends on treatment and local service capacity. Arrange early review after starting anticholinergic or beta-3 agonist therapy; continue surveillance for life after implantation of sacral nerve stimulation.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Before and after major OAB surgery, counselling and support for life should be provided by a specialist nurse or equivalent healthcare professional.

conditions.name: Stress Urinary Incontinence
conditions.description: The guideline divides SUI into uncomplicated and complicated presentations according to prior pelvic treatment, prolapse, voiding or neurological dysfunction, other lower urinary tract conditions and associated urgency symptoms.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Stress urinary incontinence may occur alone or alongside substantial storage symptoms; the latter raise the possibility of mixed urinary incontinence.

subtypes.name: uncomplicated SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No previous SUI surgery, extensive pelvic surgery or pelvic radiation; no neurogenic LUT dysfunction, bothersome genitourinary prolapse, voiding symptoms or medical condition affecting the LUT.

subtypes.name: complicated SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes previous incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic irradiation, anterior or apical pelvic-organ prolapse, voiding symptoms, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, or substantial OAB/urge urinary incontinence.

subtypes.name: recurrent SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: SUI following prior treatment; the guideline discusses surgical management as second-line treatment.

conditions.name: Mixed Urinary Incontinence
conditions.description: A broad category combining stress-related and urgency-related incontinence symptoms in different proportions; it can also encompass urodynamic SUI with detrusor overactivity or with clinical urgency but without detrusor overactivity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Stress and urgency symptoms may be equally prominent, or either may predominate.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urodynamic SUI and clinical urgency occur without demonstrated DO.

conditions.name: Underactive Bladder
conditions.description: A symptom complex involving a slow urinary stream, hesitation and straining during voiding; incomplete emptying and storage symptoms may also occur.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Women may report slow flow, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying or storage symptoms; some cannot empty the bladder adequately.

diagnostic_workup.test: Post-void residual volume (PVR) measured by ultrasound
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder emptying as part of the general evaluation of LUTS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial LUTS assessment and monitoring during treatments that may worsen voiding dysfunction.

follow_up.schedule: The interval between visits depends on patient characteristics, treatment and how frequently urinary complications occur.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The long-term natural history and clinical course of women with DU are not well established.

conditions.name: Bladder Outlet Obstruction
conditions.description: An obstruction during voiding characterised by higher detrusor pressure together with reduced urine flow.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Voiding difficulty may occur; urinary leakage can result from BOO. Persistent or progressive obstruction can be accompanied by deterioration in voiding or renal function.

subtypes.name: anatomical BOO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline distinguishes an anatomical form and recommends cysto-urethroscopy when it is suspected.

subtypes.name: functional BOO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline distinguishes a functional form, for which pelvic floor relaxation training and selected pharmacological or procedural approaches are discussed.

subtypes.name: primary bladder neck obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A cause of BOO for which bladder neck incision is discussed.

subtypes.name: urethral stricture disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A cause of BOO that may recur after treatment.

follow_up.schedule: Follow women regularly because persistent or progressive obstruction can worsen voiding or renal function; after treatment, monitor for BOO recurrence.
recommended_tests: Monitor for recurrent urethral stricture after urethral dilatation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty.
long_term_effects: Strictures may recur in the long term after urethroplasty.

conditions.name: Nocturia
conditions.description: The ICS definition from 2002 concerns waking during the night one or more times to void. Its updated quantification in 2019 counts voids during the principal sleep period, from falling asleep until intending to rise.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The person wakes to urinate during the main sleep period. The guideline distinguishes nocturia associated with nocturnal polyuria and discusses assessment for sleep disorders.

conditions.name: Pelvic organ prolapse and LUTS
conditions.description: The guideline addresses lower urinary tract symptoms and symptomatic or hidden stress urinary incontinence in women with pelvic organ prolapse.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Prolapse may coexist with LUTS or SUI, including SUI revealed only when the prolapse is reduced. SUI can newly develop after prolapse surgery.

subtypes.name: symptomatic or occult stress urinary incontinence (SUI)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Symptomatic or previously hidden SUI in women who require surgery for bothersome POP.

subtypes.name: POP without symptomatic or occult SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No symptomatic or reduction-test-detected SUI before prolapse surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect occult SUI and inform counselling about adding anti-incontinence surgery during POP surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continent women with POP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A finding of occult SUI informs discussion of the benefits and risks of combined surgery.

long_term_effects: De novo SUI can develop following prolapse surgery.

conditions.name: Urinary Fistula
conditions.description: The guideline discusses urinary tract fistulae, including upper urinary tract, urogenital, urethro-vaginal and radiation-associated fistulae, and differentiates simple from complex cases.
conditions.epidemiology: Urinary tract injury and subsequent fistula are more likely with radical surgery for malignant disease than with simpler operations for benign disease. After external beam radiotherapy for gynaecological cancer, the fistula rate appears to be of a similar order to the rate after surgery.
conditions.clinical_presentation: After pelvic surgery, fluid leakage, pelvicalyceal dilatation or high creatinine levels in drainage fluid may indicate ureteric injury or a fistula.

subtypes.name: Simple fistula with good prognosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The adapted WHO Classification of fistulae describes a single fistula < 4 cm, vesico vaginal location, uninvolved closing mechanism and ureters, no circumferential defect, little tissue loss and a first repair attempt.

subtypes.name: Complex fistula with uncertain prognosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The adapted WHO Classification of fistulae includes a fistula > 4 cm, multiple fistulae, recto-vaginal mixed or cervical fistula, closing-mechanism involvement, scarring, circumferential defect, extensive tissue loss, intravaginal ureters, failed previous repair or radiation fistula.

prognostic_tools.name: Adapted WHO Classification of fistulae

risk_groups.criteria: Single fistula < 4 cm; vesico vaginal fistula; closing mechanism uninvolved; no circumferential defect; minimal tissue loss; ureters uninvolved; first repair attempt.

Fistula > 4 cm; multiple fistulae; recto-vaginal mixed or cervical fistula; closing mechanism involved; scarring; circumferential defect; extensive tissue loss; intravaginal ureters; failed previous repair; radiation fistula.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Initially developed for obstetric fistula, this classification could also be pertinent to iatrogenic fistula.

follow_up.schedule: Maintain continuous bladder drainage after repair until healing is confirmed; expert opinion suggests ten to fourteen days for simple and/or postsurgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.
recommended_tests: Assess fistula closure and postoperative urinary incontinence separately, recording the follow-up time.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Skin care, nutrition, rehabilitation, counselling and support should be considered before and after repair as appropriate.

staging.additional_rules: Classification describes localisation (Mid-urethral, Distal, Proximal or Full length), configuration (Single, Multiloculated or Saddle shaped), communication (Mid-urethral, No communication visualised, Distal or Proximal) and continence status (Stress urinary incontinence, Continent, Post-void dribble or Mixed incontinence); these are categories rather than sequential stages.

long_term_effects: With conservative treatment, the stated risk of cancer arising inside the diverticulum is 1–6%.

therapies_index.name: prophylactic antibiotics
approved_indications: Recurrent urinary tract infections, only after discussion of the risk of increasing antimicrobial resistance.
key_toxicities: Potential to increase antimicrobial resistance.

therapies_index.name: incontinence pads
approved_indications: Temporary containment of leakage associated with OAB wet, or containment when other treatments are not planned or feasible.

therapies_index.name: containment devices
approved_indications: Containment of leakage associated with OAB wet when temporary control is needed or other treatments are not planned or feasible.

approved_indications: Management of urinary leakage resulting from BOO, but not correction of BOO.

therapies_index.name: caffeine intake
approved_indications: Reducing intake may improve urgency and frequency in adults with OAB, but not incontinence.
therapies_index.administration: Reduce intake.

therapies_index.name: fluid intake
approved_indications: Review the type and amount consumed by patients with OAB; reducing intake by 25% may improve OAB symptoms but not UI.

therapies_index.name: weight loss
approved_indications: Overweight or obese adults with OAB/UI and overweight or obese women with LUTS/SUI are encouraged to lose weight and maintain the loss.

therapies_index.name: smoking cessation strategies
approved_indications: Patients with OAB who smoke.

therapies_index.name: prompted voiding
approved_indications: Adults with OAB and cognitive impairment; short-term continence improvement has been reported in elderly people dependent on care.

therapies_index.name: bladder training
approved_indications: First-line treatment for adults with OAB/UUI or MUI.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)
approved_indications: First-line treatment for women with SUI or MUI, including elderly and pre- and postnatal women; women with urinary incontinence or other storage LUTS and nocturia; possible LUTS relief in women with POP who do not need a pessary or surgery.
therapies_index.administration: For SUI or MUI, provide supervised intensive training lasting at least three months; make programmes as intensive as possible. For nocturia, individual or group delivery is described.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) aimed at pelvic floor muscle relaxation
approved_indications: Women with functional BOO.

therapies_index.name: electrical stimulation
approved_indications: May improve OAB symptoms in some women; may be considered for SUI or to help teach pelvic floor muscle contraction.
therapies_index.administration: The type and mode of delivery for OAB vary and are poorly standardised.

therapies_index.name: posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)
approved_indications: An option for symptomatic improvement of OAB/UUI.

therapies_index.name: percutaneous-PTNS (P-PTNS)
approved_indications: OAB symptoms; a maintenance programme has demonstrated effectiveness for up to 3 years.
therapies_index.administration: A maintenance programme is described.

therapies_index.name: Transcutaneous-PTNS
approved_indications: Reduction of OAB symptoms compared with sham treatment.

therapies_index.name: anticholinergic drugs
approved_indications: Women with OAB after unsuccessful conservative treatment; urgency-predominant MUI; nocturia in women with UUI or other LUTS after counselling about benefits and risks.
therapies_index.administration: Extended-release formulations should be considered when possible. If treatment is ineffective, consider a higher dose, another formulation, or mirabegron alone or combined with an anticholinergic.
key_toxicities: Dry mouth.
Cognitive impairment.
Constipation.
Higher doses carry a greater risk of adverse effects; long-term use requires caution in elderly women, particularly those at risk of or living with cognitive dysfunction.
monitoring: Review efficacy and adverse effects early in OAB treatment.
Assess anticholinergic burden and associated comorbidities before considering treatment for OAB.

therapies_index.name: antimuscarinics
approved_indications: Treatment of OAB; the guideline also describes combining them with another treatment modality.
key_toxicities: Dry mouth is more frequent than with beta-3 agonists.
Voiding dysfunction is less frequent than with onabotulinumtoxinA.

therapies_index.name: transdermal oxybutynin
approved_indications: Treatment of OAB symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: Transdermal.
key_toxicities: Skin reactions are associated with a high withdrawal rate; dry mouth occurs less often than with oral anticholinergic drugs.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron
approved_indications: OAB symptoms; an option alone or alongside an anticholinergic when anticholinergic treatment is ineffective; additional treatment when solifenacin 5 mg provides inadequate control.
key_toxicities: The reported adverse-event rate is similar to placebo.

therapies_index.name: vibegron
approved_indications: Improvement of OAB/UUI symptoms compared with placebo.
key_toxicities: The reported adverse-event rate is similar to placebo.

therapies_index.name: beta-3 agonists
approved_indications: An alternative to anticholinergics for women with OAB after unsuccessful conservative treatment; urgency-predominant MUI.
key_toxicities: Dry mouth occurs less often than with antimuscarinics.
monitoring: Offer early follow-up after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: solifenacin
approved_indications: The guideline discusses patients with an inadequate response to solifenacin 5 mg who may benefit more from adding mirabegron than from increasing the solifenacin dose.
therapies_index.administration: 5 mg is the dose specified in the discussion of inadequate response.

therapies_index.name: vaginal oestrogen therapy
approved_indications: Women with LUTS and symptoms of genito-urinary syndrome of menopause; postmenopausal women with SUI and symptoms of vulvo vaginal atrophy.
therapies_index.administration: Vaginal.

therapies_index.name: vaginal oestrogen treatment
approved_indications: Nocturia in women, following counselling about potential benefits and risks.
therapies_index.administration: Vaginal.

therapies_index.name: oral conjugated equine oestrogen
approved_indications: Mentioned as hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in women who develop or experience worsening SUI; the guideline calls for discussion of alternative HRTs in that situation.
therapies_index.administration: Oral.
key_toxicities: Development or worsening of SUI during use is the circumstance identified for discussing alternative HRTs.

therapies_index.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
approved_indications: Bladder-wall injection for OAB/UUI refractory to conservative or drug treatment; external sphincter injection for UAB before more-invasive techniques, with disclosure that supporting evidence is low quality; intra-sphincteric injection for functional BOO.
therapies_index.administration: The specified bladder-wall dose is 100 U. Repeat bladder-wall injections may be offered when effective, subject to the manufacturer's minimum interval guidance. The document also compares sacral nerve stimulation with a 200 U detrusor injection at 24 months.
key_toxicities: Bladder-wall injections carry risks of voiding dysfunction, increased post-void residual volume and urinary tract infection.
The risk of bacteriuria after a 100 U injection is high, although its clinical significance is uncertain.
Clean intermittent self-catheterisation may be needed for a prolonged period after bladder-wall treatment.
monitoring: Discuss the limited duration of response, urinary tract infection risk and possible prolonged need for self-catheterisation before bladder-wall treatment.
Refer to the manufacturer's guidance on the minimum interval before repeat injections.

therapies_index.name: bladder wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA
approved_indications: OAB/UUI refractory to conservative therapy or drug treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Inject onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) into the bladder wall; repeat when previously effective, as needed and in accordance with the manufacturer's minimum interval guidance.
key_toxicities: Urinary tract infection.
Voiding dysfunction and increased post-void residual volume.
Possible prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation.
Bacteriuria after 100 U injection is common, but its clinical significance remains uncertain.
monitoring: Counsel patients about response duration and these risks before treatment.

therapies_index.name: onabotulinumtoxinA external sphincter injections
approved_indications: UAB before more-invasive techniques, provided patients are told that the supporting evidence is of low quality.
therapies_index.administration: External sphincter injection.

therapies_index.name: intra-sphincteric injection of onabotulinumtoxinA
approved_indications: Functional BOO in women.
therapies_index.administration: Intra-sphincteric injection.

therapies_index.name: sacral nerve stimulation
approved_indications: OAB/UUI refractory to anticholinergic therapy; UAB refractory to conservative treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Implantation is described for patients receiving treatment.
key_toxicities: Lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear are identified as implant-related concerns.
monitoring: Provide life-long surveillance of implant recipients for lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear.

therapies_index.name: sacral neuromodulation
approved_indications: Functional BOO in women.

therapies_index.name: vaginal laser therapy
approved_indications: Treatment of OAB or SUI symptoms only within a well-regulated clinical research trial; it is not offered outside that setting.
key_toxicities: Minimal short-term complications are reported for OAB treatment, but long-term safety data are lacking.

therapies_index.name: augmentation cystoplasty
approved_indications: OAB/UUI after all other treatment options have failed and the patient has been informed of possible complications.
key_toxicities: High risk of requiring clean intermittent self-catheterisation.
Small risk of malignancy.
monitoring: Provide life-long surveillance, including cystoscopic surveillance because of the small malignancy risk.
Establish before surgery that the patient is willing and able to perform clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

therapies_index.name: urinary diversion
approved_indications: OAB/UUI only after less-invasive therapies have failed, for patients who accept a stoma and have been warned of a possible small malignancy risk.
key_toxicities: Possible small risk of malignancy.

therapies_index.name: duloxetine
approved_indications: Where licensed, selected patients with SUI unresponsive to other conservative treatment who want to avoid an invasive intervention; similarly selected patients with stress-predominant MUI.
therapies_index.administration: Start and withdraw using dose titration.
key_toxicities: Potentially significant gastrointestinal and central nervous system adverse effects, with a high rate of treatment discontinuation; these effects may be limited to the first weeks of treatment.

therapies_index.name: colposuspension
approved_indications: A surgical option for SUI after discussion of risks and benefits relative to other procedures; an option to consider for complicated SUI.
therapies_index.administration: Open or laparoscopic approaches are described.

therapies_index.name: autologous sling
approved_indications: A surgical option for SUI after comparison with other procedures; an option to consider for complicated SUI.
key_toxicities: Compared with open colposuspension, higher rates of voiding dysfunction and postoperative urinary tract infection, but lower rates of POP and bladder or urethral perforation.

therapies_index.name: urethral bulking agents
approved_indications: A surgical treatment option for SUI after discussion of alternatives; an option for women requesting a low-risk procedure who understand its lower efficacy, likely need for repeat injections and unestablished long-term durability and safety; an option to consider for complicated SUI.
therapies_index.administration: Injection; repeat injections may be needed for sustained benefit. The periurethral and transurethral routes are discussed.
key_toxicities: Periurethral injection may carry a higher risk of urinary retention than transurethral injection.
Adverse-event rates are lower than with open surgery.

therapies_index.name: autologous fat
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as a urethral bulking agent that should not be offered.
key_toxicities: Higher risk of adverse events when used for urethral bulking.

therapies_index.name: hyaluronic acid
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as a urethral bulking agent that should not be offered.
key_toxicities: Higher risk of adverse events when used for urethral bulking.

therapies_index.name: mid-urethral sling (MUS)
approved_indications: An option for women seeking surgery for SUI after discussion of the relative benefits and risks of other procedures.
therapies_index.administration: Retropubic and transobturator insertion routes are discussed.
key_toxicities: The retropubic route has higher intraoperative bladder-perforation and voiding-dysfunction risks than the transobturator route.
The transobturator route has a higher groin-pain risk than the retropubic route.
Long-term mesh-related complications are a concern.
monitoring: Discuss procedural complications and all alternative treatments before surgery.

therapies_index.name: single-incision slings (Ajust® and Altis®)
approved_indications: Discussed as an SUI surgical option with apparently equivalent short-term efficacy to conventional MUS; long-term efficacy remains uncertain.
therapies_index.administration: Single-incision insertion.
key_toxicities: Compared with conventional MUS, higher rates of mesh exposure, repeat SUI surgery and dyspareunia at three years.
monitoring: Explain the uncertainty about long-term efficacy.

therapies_index.name: mechanical devices
approved_indications: Mild-to-moderate SUI after unsuccessful conservative treatment, only within a well-conducted research trial.

therapies_index.name: artificial urinary sphincter
approved_indications: An option to consider for complicated SUI; also discussed among treatments for SUI.
key_toxicities: High risk of complications, mechanical failure or explantation, even in expert centres.

therapies_index.name: adjustable compression device (ACT©)
approved_indications: Discussed as a treatment that can cure SUI, with a requirement to inform patients of its risks.
key_toxicities: High risk of complications, mechanical failure or explantation, even in expert centres.

therapies_index.name: adjustable mid urethral sling
approved_indications: Primary surgical treatment for SUI only within a well-regulated research study.

therapies_index.name: secondary synthetic sling
approved_indications: An option to consider for women with complicated SUI.
key_toxicities: For recurrent SUI, second-line surgery generally has lower efficacy and a higher complication risk than first-line use of the same procedure.

therapies_index.name: double voiding
approved_indications: Women unable to empty their bladder completely.

therapies_index.name: abdominal straining
approved_indications: Described as a technique used by some women with UAB to improve bladder emptying; the guideline calls for a warning about POP risk.
key_toxicities: Risk of POP.

therapies_index.name: clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC)
approved_indications: Standard treatment for patients unable to empty their bladder.
therapies_index.administration: Patients should receive thorough instruction in technique and risks.

therapies_index.name: indwelling transurethral catheterisation
approved_indications: Urinary drainage only when other methods have failed or are unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Indwelling transurethral catheter.

therapies_index.name: suprapubic cystostomy
approved_indications: Urinary drainage only when other methods have failed or are unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Suprapubic.

therapies_index.name: intravesical electrical stimulation
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical; routine use for UAB is not recommended.

therapies_index.name: alpha-adrenergic blockers
approved_indications: UAB, before more-invasive techniques.

therapies_index.name: intravesical prostaglandins
approved_indications: Urinary retention after surgery in women, only within well-regulated clinical trials.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical.

therapies_index.name: vaginal pessary
approved_indications: Women with grade 3 to 4 cystocoeles and BOO who are not eligible for, or do not favour, other treatment options; pessary therapy is also mentioned for POP.
therapies_index.administration: Vaginal.

therapies_index.name: clean intermittent self-dilatation
approved_indications: Women with urethral strictures or BOO following urinary incontinence surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Intermittent self-dilatation.

therapies_index.name: uroselective alpha-blockers
approved_indications: An off-label option for women with functional BOO after discussion of potential benefits and adverse events.

therapies_index.name: oral baclofen
approved_indications: Women with BOO, particularly those with increased electromyography activity and sustained detrusor contraction during voiding.
therapies_index.administration: Oral.

therapies_index.name: sildenafil
approved_indications: BOO in women only within a well-regulated clinical trial.

therapies_index.name: urethral dilatation
approved_indications: Urethral stenosis causing BOO, with advice that repeated intervention is likely; not offered for BOO after midurethral synthetic tape insertion.
key_toxicities: Theoretical risk of urethral mesh extrusion after prior midurethral synthetic tape insertion.
monitoring: Monitor for recurrent stricture after treatment.

therapies_index.name: internal urethrotomy
approved_indications: BOO caused by urethral stricture disease, with postoperative urethral self-dilatation; not offered for BOO after midurethral synthetic tape insertion.
therapies_index.administration: Follow with urethral self-dilatation.
key_toxicities: Postoperative UI.
Theoretical risk of urethral mesh extrusion after prior midurethral synthetic tape insertion.
monitoring: Explain that long-term improvement is limited to post-void residual volume and quality of life.

therapies_index.name: bladder neck incision
approved_indications: BOO secondary to primary bladder neck obstruction.
key_toxicities: Small postoperative risk of SUI, vesicovaginal fistula or urethral stricture.

therapies_index.name: urethroplasty
approved_indications: BOO due to recurrent urethral stricture after unsuccessful primary treatment.
key_toxicities: Possible long-term recurrence of stricture.
monitoring: Monitor for recurrent stricture after treatment.

therapies_index.name: urethrolysis
approved_indications: Voiding difficulties after anti-UI surgery.

therapies_index.name: sling revision
approved_indications: Urinary retention or significant voiding difficulty after tape surgery for UI.
therapies_index.administration: Options named are release, incision, partial excision or excision.
key_toxicities: Recurrent SUI and possible need for repeat or concurrent anti-UI surgery.

therapies_index.name: lifestyle advice
approved_indications: Women with LUTS, before or alongside treatment in the nocturia management section.

therapies_index.name: continuous positive airway pressure treatment
approved_indications: Women with nocturia and a history suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea should be referred for assessment of suitability at a sleep clinic.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin
approved_indications: Nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria in women after counselling about potential benefits and risks.
key_toxicities: Hyponatraemia.
monitoring: Carefully monitor serum sodium in elderly patients.
Avoid prescribing when baseline serum sodium is below the normal range.

therapies_index.name: combination of anticholinergics and desmopressin
approved_indications: Women with OAB and nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria, after counselling about potential benefits and risks.

therapies_index.name: combination of behavioural therapy and anticholinergic drugs
approved_indications: Discussed for nocturia, with advice that the combination is unlikely to be more effective than either modality alone.

therapies_index.name: timed diuretic treatment
approved_indications: Nocturia secondary to polyuria in women after counselling about potential benefits and risks.
therapies_index.administration: Timed treatment; no further schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: pelvic organ prolapse (POP) reduction test
approved_indications: Diagnostic test, rather than treatment: detection of occult SUI in continent women with POP before discussion of additional antiincontinence surgery.

therapies_index.name: simultaneous surgery for POP and SUI
approved_indications: Women requiring surgery for bothersome POP who have symptomatic or occult SUI, only after full discussion of combined surgery versus POP surgery alone.
therapies_index.administration: Combined surgery.
key_toxicities: Higher adverse-event risk than prolapse surgery alone.

therapies_index.name: concomitant antiincontinence surgery
therapies_index.administration: The guideline says not to offer it at the time of abdominal prolapse surgery to women without symptomatic or occult SUI.

therapies_index.name: ureteric stents
therapies_index.administration: Routine prophylactic use against injury during routine gynaecological surgery is not recommended.

therapies_index.name: conservative or endoluminal techniques
approved_indications: Initial management of upper urinary tract fistulae where the necessary expertise and facilities exist.

therapies_index.name: bladder drainage
approved_indications: Continuous drainage after fistula repair until healing has been confirmed.
therapies_index.administration: Expert opinion suggests ten to fourteen days for simple and/or postsurgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.

therapies_index.name: urinary and/or faecal diversions
approved_indications: Fistula repair when diversion is required.
therapies_index.administration: Avoid using irradiated tissue for repair.

therapies_index.name: interposition graft
approved_indications: Repair of radiation-associated fistulae.
therapies_index.administration: Use during fistula repair.

therapies_index.name: abdominal approach
approved_indications: Repair of persistent urogenital fistulas.
therapies_index.administration: Open, laparoscopic or robotic techniques according to availability and competence.

therapies_index.name: vaginal approach
approved_indications: Preferred approach for repair of urethro-vaginal fistulae.
therapies_index.administration: Vaginal repair.

therapies_index.name: surgical removal of symptomatic urethral diverticulum
approved_indications: Symptomatic urethral diverticulum.
key_toxicities: LUTS, including UI, can develop or persist despite technically successful removal.

therapies_index.name: urethral diverticulectomy
approved_indications: Surgical management of urethral diverticulum; bothersome concurrent SUI may be addressed at the same operation with a non-synthetic sling after counselling.
key_toxicities: Possible new or persistent LUTS, including UI, despite technically successful surgery.

therapies_index.name: concomitant non-synthetic sling
approved_indications: Bothersome SUI addressed at the time of urethral diverticulectomy after appropriate counselling.
therapies_index.administration: Placed during urethral diverticulectomy.

special_populations.population: Elderly women at risk of or living with cognitive dysfunction
special_populations.considerations: Long-term anticholinergic treatment requires particular caution. Anticholinergic burden and associated comorbidities should be assessed when considering this treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously; offer prompted voiding to adults with overactive bladder who have cognitive impairment.

special_populations.considerations: Prompted voiding, whether used alone or within a behavioural programme, improves continence in the short term.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer prompted voiding to adults with overactive bladder who have cognitive impairment.

special_populations.considerations: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not routinely be treated for the purpose of improving urinary incontinence.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not routinely give treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria with the aim of improving urinary incontinence.

special_populations.population: Elderly women with stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Surgery carries increased risks and is less likely to provide benefit. Age does not exclude women from first-line pelvic floor muscle training.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Explain the increased surgical risks and lower probability of benefit; offer supervised intensive pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months as first-line therapy.

special_populations.population: Elderly women with mixed urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: They are included among women for whom supervised intensive pelvic floor muscle training is first-line therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer supervised intensive pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months.

special_populations.considerations: Serum sodium concentration requires careful monitoring. Desmopressin should be avoided if baseline serum sodium concentration is below the normal range.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Carefully monitor serum sodium concentration and avoid prescribing desmopressin when baseline serum sodium concentration is below the normal range.

special_populations.considerations: Obesity is a risk factor for urinary incontinence in women, although its relationship with other overactive bladder symptoms is unclear. Obese women with stress urinary incontinence face greater surgical risks and a lower probability of benefit.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Encourage weight loss and maintenance of weight loss in women with overactive bladder or urinary incontinence; explain the increased risks and lower likelihood of benefit before surgery for stress urinary incontinence.

special_populations.population: Postmenopausal women with symptoms of vulvo vaginal atrophy
special_populations.considerations: The document addresses vaginal oestrogen therapy when these symptoms accompany stress urinary incontinence.

special_populations.population: Women with genito-urinary syndrome of menopause
special_populations.considerations: Associated lower urinary tract symptoms are an indication for considering vaginal oestrogen therapy.

These women are included in the first-line pelvic floor muscle training recommendation for stress urinary incontinence or mixed urinary incontinence. The mixed urinary incontinence section specifically includes postnatal women.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer supervised intensive pelvic floor muscle training lasting at least three months.

special_populations.population: Women taking oral conjugated equine oestrogen as hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
special_populations.considerations: The guidance addresses women who develop stress urinary incontinence or whose symptoms worsen while taking this treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Discuss alternative HRTs if stress urinary incontinence develops or worsens.

special_populations.population: Women with nocturia and a history suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea
special_populations.considerations: Possible sleep-disordered breathing warrants specialist assessment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer referral to a sleep clinic to assess suitability for continuous positive airway pressure treatment.

special_populations.population: Women with pelvic organ prolapse and symptomatic or occult stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Combining prolapse and anti-urinary incontinence surgery increases adverse events compared with prolapse surgery alone.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer simultaneous surgery only after discussing its potential risks and benefits compared with prolapse surgery alone.

special_populations.population: Women requiring surgery for bothersome pelvic organ prolapse without symptomatic or occult stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Stress urinary incontinence can develop after prolapse surgery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not offer concomitant antiincontinence surgery during abdominal prolapse surgery.

special_populations.considerations: Radiation fistula is classified as complex with uncertain prognosis; repair must take account of irradiated tissue.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use an interposition graft when repairing a radiation-associated fistula; avoid irradiated tissue for repair when urinary and/or faecal diversion is required. Expert opinion suggests continuous bladder drainage for fourteen to 21 days after repair of complex and/or post-radiation fistulae, until healing is confirmed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with OAB or UUI
decision_rules: Review current medicines and reassess any newly started medicine associated with the onset or worsening of OAB symptoms.
Begin with conservative measures; offer bladder training as first-line treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Bladder training
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as first-line treatment for OAB/UUI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Improves UUI in women, although its effectiveness appears lower than pharmacotherapy.

recommended_regimens.name: Pelvic floor muscle training
recommended_regimens.summary: Make training programmes as intensive as possible.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: May improve urinary frequency associated with OAB in women.

supportive_care: Explain that reducing caffeine may improve urgency and frequency, but not incontinence; recommendation grade: Strong.
Review the kind and quantity of fluid consumed; recommendation grade: Weak.
Encourage overweight or obese adults with OAB/urinary incontinence to lose weight and maintain the loss; recommendation grade: Strong.
Provide smoking-cessation strategies to smokers with OAB; recommendation grade: Strong.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A 25% reduction in fluid intake may improve OAB symptoms, but not UI; adding personalised fluid advice to pharmacotherapy provides no additional benefit for OAB.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with OAB and cognitive impairment
decision_rules: Offer prompted voiding when cognitive impairment is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Prompted voiding
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer to cognitively impaired adults with OAB.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Improves continence in the short term among elderly, care-dependent people, either alone or within a behavioural modification programme.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with OAB wet needing temporary symptom control, or for whom other treatments are not planned or feasible
decision_rules: Explain available treatments to women and/or their carers before choosing containment alone.

recommended_regimens.name: Incontinence pads and/or containment devices
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for temporary control of OAB wet or when other treatment is not planned or feasible.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Containment addresses leakage rather than replacing discussion of the available treatment options.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with OAB whose conservative treatment has failed
decision_rules: Offer anticholinergic drugs or beta-3 agonists after failure of conservative treatment.
If an anticholinergic is ineffective, consider increasing its dose, changing its formulation, or using mirabegron alone or alongside an anticholinergic.

recommended_regimens.name: Anticholinergic drugs
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer after unsuccessful conservative treatment; consider extended-release formulations whenever possible.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Compared with placebo, improve OAB symptoms, reduce urgency-incontinence episodes and daily urgency and frequency episodes, and increase mean voided volume.

recommended_regimens.name: Beta-3 agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as an alternative to anticholinergics after conservative treatment fails.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Mirabegron and vibegron improve OAB/UUI symptoms more than placebo. Beta-3 agonists are as effective as antimuscarinics for OAB, with less dry mouth.

alternative_regimens.name: mirabegron
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer as an additional treatment when solifenacin 5 mg has provided inadequate control; recommendation grade: Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Patients inadequately treated with solifenacin 5 mg may benefit more from adding mirabegron than from increasing the solifenacin dose.

alternative_regimens.name: Transdermal oxybutynin
alternative_regimens.summary: Has less dry mouth than oral anticholinergic drugs, but discontinuation due to skin reactions is frequent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative anticholinergic formulation may be considered when treatment is ineffective.

response_assessment.method: Review efficacy and adverse effects of anticholinergic therapy; arrange early follow-up after anticholinergic or beta-3 agonist initiation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Higher anticholinergic doses improve OAB symptoms more but increase adverse effects. Extended-release formulations cause fewer adverse events than immediate-release preparations. Anticholinergic adherence is low and declines with time because of insufficient efficacy, adverse events and/or cost; most patients stop within the first three months. The source describes similar adverse-event rates for mirabegron and vibegron and placebo.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Elderly women, particularly those with existing cognitive dysfunction or at risk of it, being considered for long-term anticholinergic treatment
decision_rules: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously in this population.
Assess anticholinergic burden and associated comorbidities when considering anticholinergic therapy.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Caution with long-term anticholinergic treatment is Strong; assessment of anticholinergic burden and comorbidities is Weak. Anticholinergic drugs have more adverse events than placebo, including cognitive impairment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with symptomatic OAB/UUI
decision_rules: Consider posterior tibial nerve stimulation for symptomatic improvement.

recommended_regimens.name: Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider as an option for improving OAB/UUI symptoms.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reduces UUI episodes more effectively than antimuscarinics, without a difference in other OAB symptoms. Transcutaneous-PTNS appears more effective than sham treatment for OAB symptoms and is not inferior to P-PTNS for urgency, frequency and quality-of-life scores.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence level 2a indicates that a maintenance programme of P-PTNS has been effective for up to 3 years. Electrical stimulation may help some women, but its delivery methods remain variable and poorly standardised.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with LUTS accompanied by symptoms of genito-urinary syndrome of menopause
decision_rules: Offer vaginal oestrogen therapy when these symptoms coexist.

recommended_regimens.name: Vaginal oestrogen therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for LUTS associated with symptoms of genito-urinary syndrome of menopause.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with OAB/UUI refractory to conservative or drug treatment
decision_rules: Offer bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA injections when conservative therapy or medication has not controlled OAB/UUI.
Discuss the limited duration of benefit, urinary tract infection risk and possible prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation before treatment.
If injections have worked, offer further injections when needed, observing the manufacturer's minimum interval.

recommended_regimens.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer bladder-wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U).
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: One bladder-wall treatment with 100 U is more effective than placebo for curing or improving UUI/OAB symptoms and improving quality of life. Compared with antimuscarinics, it cures UUI more effectively but reduces mean UUI episodes similarly.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Repeat injections as required after an effective treatment; follow the manufacturer's guidance on the minimum interval.

response_assessment.method: Assess whether the previous injection was effective and whether retreatment is needed.
response_assessment.interpretation: Repeat treatment may be offered when the earlier injection was effective.

supportive_care: Counsel about urinary tract infection, voiding dysfunction and the potential for prolonged clean intermittent self-catheterisation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Injections can cause increased PVR and voiding dysfunction. Bacteriuria risk after onabotA (100 U) is high, but its clinical significance remains uncertain. There is no evidence that repeated injections lose efficacy, although discontinuation is frequent.

recommended_regimens.name: Sacral nerve stimulation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for OAB/UUI refractory to anticholinergic treatment.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: More effective than continuing unsuccessful conservative treatment, although sham controls were not used; as effective as onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U detrusor injection at 24 months. Among implanted patients, a 50% improvement in UUI persists in ≥ 50%, and 15% may remain cured at 4 years; evidence level 3 for these longer-term results.

response_assessment.method: Monitor the implant for lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear.

recommended_regimens.name: Colposuspension
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer open or laparoscopic colposuspension after discussing its risks and benefits against other operations.

recommended_regimens.name: Autologous sling
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer placement after comparing risks and benefits with other surgical approaches.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Associated with high cure rates and a higher cure rate than colposuspension.

recommended_regimens.name: Mid-urethral sling (MUS)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer after discussing comparative risks and benefits, mesh-related complications and alternatives.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Retropubic MUS appears to provide better patient-reported subjective and objective SUI cure than colposuspension. Retropubic and transobturator synthetic MUS have equivalent patient-reported outcomes at one year; longer-term patient-reported cure is higher with the retropubic approach.

recommended_regimens.name: Urethral bulking agents
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer after comparing surgical options; also offer to women seeking a low-risk procedure who understand its lower efficacy, likely need for further injections and unestablished long-term durability and safety.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: May achieve short-term improvement or cure, but cure is less likely than with MUS, colposuspension or autologous sling.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Repeat injections may be needed to maintain benefit.

not_recommended.name: Autologous fat and hyaluronic acid
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer as urethral bulking agents because of their higher adverse-event risk; recommendation grade: Strong.

not_recommended.name: Vaginal laser therapy
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer for SUI symptoms outside a well-regulated clinical research trial; recommendation grade: Strong.

response_assessment.method: Evaluate efficacy and identify early postoperative complications.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Autologous sling has an overall adverse-event rate similar to open colposuspension, with more voiding dysfunction and postoperative urinary tract infections but less pelvic organ prolapse and bladder or urethral perforation. Bulking agents have fewer adverse events than open surgery; periurethral injection may cause more urinary retention than transurethral injection. There is no evidence that one bulking-agent type is better than another.

recommended_regimens.name: Mid-urethral sling (MUS)
recommended_regimens.summary: Discuss route-specific outcomes and harms before selecting a sling.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: MUS cohorts showed sustained response beyond ten years; evidence level 2b. Retropubic insertion has higher longer-term patient-reported cure than transobturator insertion; evidence level 1b.

alternative_regimens.name: Ajust® and Altis®
alternative_regimens.summary: Single-incision slings have non-inferior comparative efficacy against conventional MUS at fifteen and 36 months, while long-term efficacy remains uncertain.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: If a single-incision sling is offered, counsel about the higher rates of mesh exposure, repeat SUI surgery and dyspareunia at three years compared with conventional MUS.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Retropubic insertion entails more intraoperative bladder perforation and voiding dysfunction than transobturator insertion, while transobturator insertion entails more groin pain. For single-incision slings, insertion takes less time than with standard retropubic slings, and blood loss and immediate postoperative pain are lower than with conventional MUS.
