document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: The guideline has broadened its focus from urinary incontinence (UI) to nonneurogenic female lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), bringing women with functional urological conditions that do not necessarily involve UI within its scope. Added subjects include non-obstetric fistulae, female bladder outlet obstruction [BOO], underactive bladder [UAB] and nocturia. The scope may expand further over the next two or three iterations.

document_sections.heading: History and physical examination
document_sections.content: A clinical history is considered the first step in assessing LUTS, despite the absence of high-level supporting evidence. It should cover storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms; sexual, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms; urgency episodes; and the type, timing, severity and approximate quantity of UI. The history helps classify LUTS by symptom phase and UI as stress urinary incontinence (SUI), urgency UI (UUI), mixed UI (MUI) or overflow incontinence. Overflow incontinence denotes reported UI alongside symptoms of an excessively full bladder without an identified cause. Recommendation (Strong): obtain a comprehensive history covering symptoms and comorbidities and perform a focused examination in women with LUTS.

document_sections.heading: Patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: validated condition-specific scores help screen for and classify LUTS (LE 3); validated symptom scores quantify UI and LUTS severity (LE 3); condition-specific and general health questionnaires assess present health and detect treatment-related change (LE 3); questionnaires cannot substitute for a detailed consultation and belong within a full history (LE 4). Recommendation (Strong): include a suitable validated questionnaire in standardized initial assessment and follow-up of female LUTS.

document_sections.heading: Bladder diaries
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): ask patients with LUTS to keep a bladder diary during standardized assessment of female LUTS, and use a diary lasting ≥ 3 days.

document_sections.heading: Urinalysis
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): include urinalysis in the initial LUTS assessment; if urinary tract infection is present, reassess LUTS after treating it; do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly patients for the purpose of improving UI.

document_sections.heading: Post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): measure post-void residual volume (PVR) at the initial assessment of patients with LUTS, use ultrasound for that measurement, and monitor PVR during treatments that might cause or aggravate voiding dysfunction. Recommendation (Weak): additionally assess bladder voiding efficiency when measuring PVR.

document_sections.heading: Urodynamics
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: urodynamics can comprehensively characterize LUT function across clinical conditions (LE 4), although most parameters vary within a session and over time (LE 3). Urethral-function measurement methods can have good repeatability but do not consistently agree with other urodynamic tests or UI severity (LE 3); clinical history and urodynamic findings can disagree (LE 3). A urodynamic finding of detrusor overactivity (DO) does not affect overactive bladder treatment outcomes (LE 1a). Preoperative testing does not improve SUI surgical outcomes in women with uncomplicated, clinically demonstrable SUI (LE 1b). Urethral-function results do not consistently predict SUI surgical success or failure (LE 3), and evidence does not consistently link preoperative DO to failure of MUI surgery (LE 3). Preoperative DO may be associated with persistent urgency after SUI surgery (LE 3). Recommendations (Strong): follow International Continence Society good-practice standards; do not routinely test before treating uncomplicated SUI or before first-line treatment of uncomplicated overactive bladder symptoms; do not grade UI severity using urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure. Recommendation (Weak): perform urodynamics when its findings might alter the choice of invasive treatment.

document_sections.heading: Pad testing
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): if conducting a pad test, standardize its duration and activity protocol. Recommendation (Weak): use pad testing when UI needs quantification, particularly for evaluating treatment response.

document_sections.heading: Imaging
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): do not routinely image the upper or lower urinary tract during LUTS assessment.

document_sections.heading: Urinary biomarkers
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): do not routinely use urinary biomarkers or urinary microbiome estimates to diagnose or manage LUT disease in women.

document_sections.heading: DISEASE MANAGEMENT Overactive bladder
document_sections.content: The International Continence Society defines overactive bladder by urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urge UI, when urinary tract infection (UTI) and other evident pathology are absent.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: For overactive bladder (OAB), recommendations (Strong) are to obtain a bladder diary covering at least three days at initial assessment and not to perform urodynamics routinely before first-line treatment of uncomplicated OAB symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Conservative management Addressing underlying disease/cognitive impairment
document_sections.content: LUTS, particularly among elderly people, have been associated with cardiac failure, chronic renal failure, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, neurological disease, general cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances such as sleep apnoea, depression and metabolic syndrome.

document_sections.heading: Conservative management of overactive bladder
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): document current medications in every patient with OAB and review newly introduced medicines linked to the onset or worsening of OAB symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Urinary containment
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): explain available treatments to women with OAB and/or their carers before choosing containment alone; provide incontinence pads and/or containment devices for OAB wet as a temporary measure or when other treatment is not intended or feasible; offer prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent UTI only after discussing the risk of greater antimicrobial resistance.

document_sections.heading: Lifestyle interventions
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: reducing caffeine may lessen frequency and urgency (LE 2). Decreasing fluid consumption by 25% may improve OAB symptoms but not UI (LE 1b); individualized fluid advice adds no benefit to pharmacotherapy for OAB (LE 2). Obesity increases women's UI risk, while its relationship with other OAB symptoms is unclear (LE 1b). Evidence that smoking cessation improves OAB symptoms is weak (LE 3). Recommendations: explain that caffeine reduction may improve urgency and frequency, but not incontinence (Strong); review fluid type and quantity (Weak); encourage overweight and obese adults with OAB/UI to lose weight and sustain the loss (Strong); provide smoking-cessation strategies to smokers with OAB (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Behavioural and physical therapies
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: prompted voiding, alone or within behavioural modification, improves short-term continence in elderly care-dependent people (LE 1b). Bladder training improves women's UUI, seemingly less effectively than pharmacotherapy (LE 1b). Pelvic floor muscle training may lessen OAB-related frequency (LE 1b). Electrical stimulation may benefit some women, although its methods and delivery are variable and poorly standardized (LE 1a). Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) reduces UUI episodes more than antimuscarinics, without a difference for other OAB symptoms (LE 1a). Maintenance percutaneous-PTNS (P-PTNS) has demonstrated effectiveness for up to 3 years (LE 2a). Transcutaneous-PTNS appears effective against OAB symptoms relative to sham treatment (LE 1a) and is not inferior to P-PTNS for urgency, frequency and quality-of-life scores (LE 1a). Recommendations (Strong): offer prompted voiding to cognitively impaired adults with OAB; use bladder training first-line for adults with OAB/UUI; make pelvic floor muscle training as intensive as possible; consider PTNS to improve OAB/UUI symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacological management Anticholinergic drugs
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: relative to placebo, anticholinergic drugs improve OAB symptoms, reduce urgency-incontinence episodes and daily urgency and frequency, and increase average voided volume (LE 1a), but produce more adverse events, including dry mouth, cognitive impairment and constipation (LE 1a). Once-daily extended-release products have fewer adverse events than immediate-release products (LE 1b). Transdermal oxybutynin causes less dry mouth than oral anticholinergic drugs but has substantial withdrawal due to skin reactions (LE 1b). Higher doses improve symptoms more while increasing adverse-effect risk (LE 1a). No individual anticholinergic is clearly superior for curing or improving OAB/UUI (LE 1a). Combining antimuscarinics with another treatment improves OAB more than antimuscarinics alone (LE 1a). Adherence is low and falls over time because of insufficient efficacy, adverse events and/or cost (LE 2a); most patients discontinue within the first three months (LE 2a). Recommendations (Strong): offer anticholinergic drugs after conservative treatment fails; consider extended-release preparations where possible; after ineffective therapy, consider a higher dose, another anticholinergic formulation, or mirabegron alone or alongside an anticholinergic; review effectiveness and adverse effects early.

document_sections.heading: Beta-3 agonists Mirabegron
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: mirabegron and vibegron improve OAB/UUI symptoms more than placebo (LE 1a), with adverse-event rates similar to placebo (LE 1a). Beta-3 agonists have OAB effectiveness comparable to antimuscarinics and lower dry-mouth rates (LE 1a). For patients inadequately treated with solifenacin 5 mg, adding mirabegron may benefit them more than raising the solifenacin dose (LE 1b). Recommendation (Strong): offer beta-3 agonists instead of anticholinergics to women whose OAB persists after conservative treatment. Recommendation (Weak): add mirabegron for patients inadequately treated with solifenacin 5 mg.

document_sections.heading: Anticholinergics and beta-3 agonists: the elderly and cognition
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): use long-term anticholinergic therapy cautiously in elderly women, particularly those with existing cognitive dysfunction or at risk of it. Recommendation (Weak): evaluate anticholinergic burden and related comorbidities before anticholinergic treatment for overactive bladder syndrome.

document_sections.heading: Oestrogens
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Weak): offer vaginal oestrogen therapy to women whose LUTS coexist with symptoms of genito-urinary syndrome of menopause.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management Bladder wall injection of onabotulinumtoxinA
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: one bladder-wall injection treatment with onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) (100 U) is more effective than placebo for curing or improving UUI/OAB symptoms and improving quality of life (LE 1a). Reduced effectiveness with repeated injections has not been demonstrated, although discontinuation is frequent (LE 2a). Injections carry risks of voiding dysfunction, increased post-void residual volume and UTI (LE 1a). Bacteriuria risk following onabotA (100 U) is high, but its clinical significance is uncertain (LE 1b). Compared with antimuscarinics, onabotulinumtoxinA cures UUI more effectively, reduces average UUI episodes similarly and causes more voiding dysfunction (LE 1a for each comparison). Recommendations (Strong): offer bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) for OAB/UUI refractory to conservative or drug treatment; before treatment, discuss its limited response duration, UTI risk and possible prolonged requirement for clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

document_sections.heading: Sacral nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: Sacral Nerve Stimulation (SNS) outperforms continued unsuccessful conservative treatment for OAB/UUI, although sham controls were not used (LE 1b). Its effectiveness equals that of onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U detrusor injection at 24 months (LE 1b). Among implant recipients, a 50% improvement in UUI persists in ≥ 50% of patients, and 15% may remain cured at 4 years (LE 3). Recommendation (Strong): offer sacral nerve stimulation for OAB/UUI refractory to anticholinergic therapy.

document_sections.heading: Laser treatment
document_sections.content: Vaginal laser therapy produces minimal short-term improvement in OAB symptoms with minimal complications; long-term effectiveness and safety data are lacking (LE 3). Recommendation (Strong): do not offer it for OAB symptoms outside a well-regulated clinical research trial.

document_sections.heading: Cystoplasty/urinary diversion
document_sections.content: Recommendations: arrange specialist-nurse or equivalent counselling and life-long support before and after major OAB surgery (Strong); offer augmentation cystoplasty only after all other options have failed and possible complications have been explained (Weak); warn cystoplasty candidates of a high likelihood of clean intermittent self-catheterisation, confirm their willingness and ability to perform it, and explain the need for life-long surveillance (Strong); do not offer detrusor myectomy for UUI (Weak); reserve urinary diversion for OAB/UUI after less-invasive options fail, when the patient accepts a stoma and has been informed of the possible small malignancy risk (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: OAB follow-up depends on treatment and local service capacity, making uniform pathways difficult; panel recommendations draw on best practice and clinical-trial standards. Recommendations: arrange early follow-up after starting anticholinergic or beta-3 agonist treatment (Strong); repeat effective onabotulinumtoxinA injections when needed, observing the manufacturer's guidance on the minimum interval (Strong); provide life-long surveillance after a sacral nerve stimulation implant for lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear (Strong); offer cystoscopic surveillance after augmentation cystoplasty because of the small malignancy risk (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Stress Urinary Incontinence
document_sections.content: This part addresses classification, diagnosis, conservative and pharmacological care, surgery and follow-up for stress urinary incontinence.

document_sections.heading: Classification
document_sections.content: The Panel's consensus distinguishes uncomplicated from complicated SUI. Uncomplicated SUI excludes previous SUI surgery, extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic radiation, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, bothersome genitourinary prolapse, voiding symptoms and medical conditions affecting the LUT. Substantial additional storage symptoms, particularly OAB, warrant consideration of MUI. Complicated SUI includes previous incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic irradiation, anterior or apical pelvic-organ prolapse, voiding symptoms, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, or significant OAB/UUI.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic evaluation History taking and physical examination
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): for every woman presenting with SUI, obtain a complete clinical history and perform a thorough examination, including a standardized cough test.

document_sections.heading: Patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): incorporate an appropriate validated questionnaire into standardized assessment of SUI.

document_sections.heading: Post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): measure PVR, especially when voiding symptoms or complicated SUI are present; favor ultrasound over catheterisation for measurement; and monitor PVR before treatments that could cause or worsen voiding dysfunction, including SUI surgery.

document_sections.heading: Urodynamics
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: preoperative urodynamics do not improve surgical results for uncomplicated, clinically demonstrable SUI (LE 1b). Urethral-function tests do not consistently predict success or failure of SUI surgery (LE 3). Evidence does not consistently associate preoperative detrusor overactivity with failure of mid-urethral sling (MUS) surgery (LE 3). Recommendations (Weak): perform preoperative testing when SUI accompanies storage symptoms, incontinence type is unclear, voiding dysfunction is suspected, pelvic organ prolapse is present, or prior SUI surgery has occurred; also test if results might change invasive-treatment selection. Recommendation (Strong): do not grade incontinence severity with urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure, which chiefly assess urethral function.

document_sections.heading: Imaging
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): do not routinely image the upper or lower urinary tract when assessing SUI.

document_sections.heading: Disease management Conservative management Obesity and weight loss
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): encourage overweight and obese women with LUTS/SUI to lose weight and maintain that loss.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: Recommendations: offer supervised, intensive pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) for at least three months as first-line treatment to all women with SUI or MUI, including elderly and pre- and postnatal women (Strong); make PFMT programmes as intensive as possible (Strong); weigh PFMT effectiveness and absence of adverse events against the expected effects and complications of invasive SUI surgery (Strong); consider electrical stimulation for SUI treatment or to help teach PFM contraction (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Pharmacological management Oestrogens
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): offer vaginal oestrogen to postmenopausal women with SUI and vulvo vaginal atrophy symptoms; discuss other HRTs with women whose SUI begins or worsens while they take oral conjugated equine oestrogen as hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

document_sections.heading: Duloxetine
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: duloxetine improves women's SUI, but cure is unlikely (LE 1a). It may produce substantial gastrointestinal and central nervous system effects and frequent discontinuation, although these effects may be confined to the first weeks of therapy (LE 1a). Recommendations (Strong): where licensed, offer duloxetine to selected patients who remain symptomatic after other conservative treatments and wish to avoid invasive treatment, after careful adverse-event counselling; titrate the dose when starting and stopping because adverse-event risk is high.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management General considerations
document_sections.content: Long-term complication concerns have led to scrutiny of polypropylene mesh used for synthetic mid-urethral slings (MUS); some European countries, including the United Kingdom, have paused their use. A 2020 UK parliamentary review reported that many women benefit without difficulty, but others have suffered severe complications. It noted that the true number affected is unknown and emphasized support for affected women and learning from their experiences.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management of uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): after conservative options have been explored or have failed, offer an appropriate choice of surgical procedures and discuss each one's advantages and disadvantages; restrict new SUI devices to structured research, with results tracked in a registry or well-regulated trial; use shared decision-making to select treatment.

document_sections.heading: Open and laparoscopic colposuspension surgery
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): offer open or laparoscopic colposuspension to women seeking SUI surgery after thoroughly discussing its risks and benefits relative to other surgical options.

document_sections.heading: Autologous sling
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: autologous slings have high SUI cure rates (LE 1a) and cure more often than colposuspension (LE 1a). Overall adverse-event rates are similar to open colposuspension, but voiding dysfunction and postoperative UTI are more frequent, whereas pelvic organ prolapse and bladder or urethral perforation are less frequent (LE 1a). Recommendation (Strong): offer an autologous sling to women seeking SUI surgery after a thorough comparison of risks and benefits with other procedures.

document_sections.heading: Urethral bulking agents
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: bulking agents may improve or cure SUI in the short term (LE 1b), but cure less often than MUS, colposuspension or autologous sling, and sustained benefit may require repeat injections (LE 1b). Autologous fat and hyaluronic acid have greater adverse-event risk (LE 1a). Bulking agents cause fewer adverse events than open surgery (LE 2a). No evidence favors one bulking agent over another (LE 1b). Periurethral injection may carry more urinary-retention risk than transurethral injection (LE 2b). Recommendations (Strong): offer bulking agents after discussing their risks and benefits against other SUI operations; offer them to women preferring a low-risk procedure while explaining their lower effectiveness, likely repeat injections and unestablished long-term durability and safety; do not offer autologous fat or hyaluronic acid because of higher adverse-event risk.

document_sections.heading: Laser treatment
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): do not offer vaginal laser therapy for SUI symptoms outside a well-regulated clinical research trial.

document_sections.heading: Mid-urethral slings
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: retropubic MUS appears to achieve better patient-reported subjective and objective SUI cure than colposuspension (LE 1a). Transobturator and retropubic synthetic MUS yield equivalent patient-reported outcomes at one year (LE 1a), while retropubic insertion has higher longer-term patient-reported cure (LE 1b). MUS cohorts show sustained benefit beyond ten years (LE 2b). Compared with transobturator insertion, retropubic insertion has higher intraoperative bladder-perforation and voiding-dysfunction risks (LE 1a); transobturator insertion has more groin pain (LE 1a). For transobturator insertion, skin-to-vagina (outside-in) and vagina-to-skin (inside-out) have comparable effectiveness up to nine years (LE 2a). Top-to-bottom (inside-out) retropubic insertion has greater postoperative voiding-dysfunction risk (LE 1b). Ajust® and Altis® singleincision slings are non inferior to conventional MUS for comparative effectiveness at fifteen and 36 months (LE 1b). Single-incision MUS takes less operating time than standard retropubic sling insertion (LE 1b), with less blood loss and immediate postoperative pain than conventional MUS (LE 1b), but Ajust® and Altis® have higher mesh-exposure, repeat-SUI-surgery and dyspareunia rates at three years (LE 1b). Evidence does not establish whether other surgical adverse outcomes differ (LE 1b). Coital incontinence is likely to improve after SUI surgery (LE 3); evidence on overall sexual function is conflicting (LE 1a). Recommendations (Strong): offer MUS after comparing it with other operations; explain superior long-term retropubic outcomes versus transobturator outcomes; discuss MUS complications and all alternatives in light of concerns about surgical mesh; explain that short-term effectiveness of Ajust® and Altis® seems equivalent to conventional MUS and that long-term effectiveness of single-incision slings remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Other treatments of uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): offer mechanical devices to women with mild-to-moderate SUI after failed conservative treatment only within a well-conducted research trial. Explain to candidates for artificial urinary sphincter or adjustable compression device (ACT©) that cure is possible, but complications, mechanical failure or explantation remain high risks even in expert centres.

document_sections.heading: Management of complicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Recommendations: limit management of complicated SUI to suitably experienced centres (Strong); choose recurrent-SUI surgery after careful assessment of individual factors, considering cystoscopy and multichannel urodynamics when appropriate (Strong); explain that second-line surgery generally has lower effectiveness and more complications than first-line use of the same procedure (Weak); offer an adjustable mid urethral sling as primary SUI surgery only in a well-regulated research study (Strong); consider secondary synthetic sling, bulking agents, colposuspension, autologous sling or artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) for complicated SUI (Weak); warn candidates for AUS or ACT® that, despite possible cure, complications, mechanical failure and explantation are substantial risks even in expert centres (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Surgery of stress urinary incontinence in special patient groups
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Weak): tell obese women with SUI that surgery entails increased risks and a lower chance of benefit; give older women with SUI the same warning about increased risk and likely lower probability of benefit.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: SUI follow-up varies by treatment. Allow adequate time to observe effects of conservative and physical treatment; arrange early review after pharmacological treatment; and, for most operations, arrange short-term review to evaluate effectiveness and detect early postoperative complications.

document_sections.heading: Mixed Urinary Incontinence
document_sections.content: MUI encompasses equally prominent stress and urgency symptoms, predominantly stress or predominantly urgency symptoms, urodynamic SUI (USUI or USI) with detrusor overactivity (DO), and USUI with clinical urgency but no DO.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: No evidence shows that urodynamics changes MUI treatment outcomes (LE 3). Recommendations: take a thorough history and perform an examination (Strong); identify stresspredominant or urgency-predominant MUI where possible (Weak); use bladder diaries and urodynamics within multimodal assessment to guide management (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Disease Management Conservative management in mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: PFMT appears less effective for MUI than for SUI alone (LE 2), but improves incontinence and quality of life compared with no treatment (LE 1a). Bladder training combined with PFMT may help (LE 1b). Recommendations: address the most bothersome symptom first (Weak); offer bladder training first-line to adults with MUI (Strong); offer all women with MUI, including elderly and postnatal women, supervised intensive pelvic floor muscle training lasting at least three months as first-line therapy (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Pharmacological management of mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Recommendations: treat the most bothersome symptom first (Weak); offer anticholinergic drugs or beta-3 agonists for urgency-predominant MUI (Strong); where licensed, offer duloxetine to selected patients with stress-predominant MUI who have not responded to other conservative approaches and prefer to avoid invasive treatment, with careful adverse-event counselling (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Surgical management of mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Recommendations: address the most bothersome symptom first (Weak); warn that MUI surgery succeeds less often than surgery for SUI alone (Strong); explain that one treatment might not resolve all incontinence and that other components may also need treatment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Underactive Bladder
document_sections.content: The ICS describes underactive bladder as a symptom complex involving slow urinary flow, hesitancy and straining, sometimes with incomplete-emptying sensation and storage symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Management of underactive bladder
document_sections.content: Recommendations: encourage double voiding for women unable to empty fully (Weak); warn women with underactive bladder (UAB) who strain abdominally to empty about pelvic organ prolapse (POP) risk (Weak); use clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC) as standard treatment when bladder emptying is not possible and thoroughly teach its technique and risks (Strong for both); reserve indwelling transurethral catheterisation or suprapubic cystostomy for failure or unsuitability of other drainage methods (Weak); do not routinely recommend intravesical electrical stimulation (Weak) or parasympathomimetics (Strong) for UAB; offer alpha-adrenergic blockers before more-invasive techniques (Weak); offer intravesical prostaglandins for postoperative urinary retention only in well-regulated clinical trials (Weak); before more-invasive approaches, offer onabotulinumtoxinA external sphincter injections if patients understand the supporting evidence is low quality (Weak); offer sacral nerve stimulation after conservative treatment fails (Strong); do not routinely offer detrusor myoplasty for detrusor underactivity (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: The natural history and long-term clinical course of women with DU are not well known. Visit intervals depend on patient characteristics, the treatment delivered and how often urinary complications occur.

document_sections.heading: Bladder Outlet Obstruction
document_sections.content: The ICS defines bladder outlet obstruction by obstruction during voiding accompanied by increased detrusor pressure and reduced urine flow.

document_sections.heading: Classification of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): classify female bladder outlet obstruction consistently as anatomical or functional, and fully characterize research populations using that classification.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): obtain a full history and thorough clinical examination for suspected bladder outlet obstruction (BOO); do not diagnose female BOO from flow-study measurements alone; perform cysto-urethroscopy when anatomical BOO is suspected; and perform urodynamic evaluation for suspected BOO.

document_sections.heading: Conservative treatment of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Recommendations: offer pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) focused on relaxation for functional BOO (Weak); prioritize research into how PFMT affects coordinated pelvic-floor relaxation during voiding (Strong); offer a vaginal pessary to women with grade 3 to 4 cystocoeles and BOO who cannot or do not wish to pursue other options (Weak); offer containment devices for BOO-related leakage without presenting them as correction of the obstruction (Weak); offer clean intermittent self-dilatation for urethral strictures or BOO after UI surgery (Weak); do not offer an intraurethral device for BOO (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Pharmacologic treatment of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Recommendations: after discussing possible benefits and adverse events, offer uroselective alpha-blockers off-label for functional BOO (Weak); offer oral baclofen for BOO, particularly with increased electromyography activity and sustained detrusor contraction during voiding (Weak); restrict sildenafil for BOO to well-regulated clinical trials (Strong); do not offer thyrotropin-releasing hormone for BOO (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Surgical treatment of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Recommendations: offer intra-sphincteric onabotulinumtoxinA or sacral neuromodulation for functional BOO (Weak for each); advise that prolapse-associated voiding symptoms may improve after surgery (Weak); offer urethral dilatation for obstructing urethral stenosis while explaining that repetition will probably be needed (Weak); offer internal urethrotomy followed by self-dilatation for obstructing urethral stricture while explaining limited long-term improvement and postoperative UI risk (Weak); do not use urethral dilatation or urethrotomy for BOO after midurethral synthetic tape insertion because of a theoretical urethral mesh-extrusion risk (Weak); explain that long-term improvements after internal urethrotomy are limited to PVR and quality of life (Weak); offer bladder neck incision for primary bladder neck obstruction (Weak) and warn about small postoperative risks of SUI, vesicovaginal fistula or urethral stricture (Strong); offer urethroplasty after failed primary treatment for recurrent urethral stricture (Weak), explaining possible long-term recurrence (Weak); offer urethrolysis for voiding difficulty after anti-UI surgery (Weak); offer sling revision by release, incision, partial excision or excision for retention or significant voiding difficulty following UI tape surgery (Strong), with warning about recurrent SUI and possible repeat or simultaneous anti-UI surgery (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: Monitor women with BOO regularly because persistent or progressive obstruction may further impair voiding or renal function. After treatment, check for recurrent obstruction; after urethral dilation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty for stricture, specifically monitor for stricture recurrence.

document_sections.heading: Nocturia
document_sections.content: The ICS definition from 2002 describes waking from sleep at night one or more times to void. Its updated 2019 quantification counts voids during the main sleep period, from falling asleep until intending to rise.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis of nocturia
document_sections.content: Recommendations: obtain a full medical history, including sleep-disorder screening (Strong); use a validated questionnaire for assessment and reassessment during and/or after treatment (Weak); use a three-day bladder diary (Strong), not a nocturnal-only diary (Weak); when nocturia predominates, consider sleep-disorder screening and blood tests for renal function, thyroid function, HbA1c and calcium at initial workup (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Conservative management of nocturia
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): offer lifestyle advice to women with LUTS before or alongside treatment; offer individual or group pelvic floor muscle training for nocturia when UI or other storage LUTS coexist; refer women whose history suggests obstructive sleep apnoea to a sleep clinic to assess suitability for continuous positive airway pressure.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacological management of nocturia
document_sections.content: Recommendations: offer desmopressin for nocturia caused by nocturnal polyuria after counselling on benefits and risks, including hyponatraemia (Strong); monitor serum sodium carefully in elderly recipients and avoid desmopressin when baseline sodium is below the normal range (Strong); offer anticholinergic treatment for nocturia with UUI or other LUTS after benefit-and-risk counselling (Strong); explain that combining behavioural therapy with anticholinergics is unlikely to work better than either alone (Weak); after appropriate counselling, offer anticholinergics with desmopressin for OAB with nocturia caused by nocturnal polyuria (Weak), vaginal oestrogen for nocturia (Weak), or timed diuretics for nocturia caused by polyuria (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: The underlying cause of nocturia and the treatment used determine follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Detection of stress urinary incontinence in women with pelvic organ prolapse
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): perform a pelvic organ prolapse (POP) reduction test in continent women to detect occult SUI, then discuss advantages and disadvantages of adding antiincontinence surgery during POP surgery.

document_sections.heading: Conservative treatment of pelvic organ prolapse and LUTS
document_sections.content: Recommendations (Strong): tell women with POP who do not require a pessary or surgery that PFMT may relieve LUTS; do not offer preoperative PFMT to improve LUTS outcomes when pessary treatment or POP surgery is indicated.

document_sections.heading: Surgery for bothersome pelvic organ prolapse
document_sections.content: For women requiring surgery for bothersome POP who have symptomatic or occult SUI, offer simultaneous POP and SUI surgery only after fully comparing its risks and benefits with POP surgery alone (Strong), and explain the greater adverse-event risk of combined surgery (Strong). For women without symptomatic or occult SUI, explain the risk of new SUI after prolapse surgery (Strong) and do not offer simultaneous antiincontinence surgery during abdominal prolapse surgery (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology of urinary fistula
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries: urinary-tract injury followed by fistula is more likely after radical surgery for malignant disease than after simple surgery for benign disease (LE 2). Fistula formation following external beam radiotherapy for gynaecological cancer appears to occur at a rate of the same order as following surgery (LE 4).

document_sections.heading: Adapted WHO Classification of fistulae*
document_sections.content: The classification table distinguishes simple fistula with good prognosis from complex fistula with uncertain prognosis. Simple features are a single fistula < 4 cm, vesico vaginal location, intact closing mechanism, absence of a circumferential defect, minimal tissue loss, no ureteric involvement and a first repair attempt. Complex features are a fistula > 4 cm, multiple fistulae, recto-vaginal mixed or cervical fistula, closing-mechanism involvement, scarring, a circumferential defect, extensive tissue loss, intravaginal ureters, previous failed repair or radiation-associated fistula. Although developed initially for obstetric fistula, the classification may also apply to iatrogenic fistula.

document_sections.heading: Classification of urinary fistula
document_sections.content: Recommendation (Strong): use a urinary-tract fistula classification system to promote consistent terminology.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic evaluation of urinary fistula
document_sections.content: Recommendations: take a complete history and conduct a focused examination with direct visual inspection when urinary fistula is suspected (Strong); use cystoscopy and retrograde filling of the bladder with coloured fluid for confirmation (Weak); use contrast-enhanced computed tomography with a late excretory phase or magnetic resonance imaging when diagnosis is difficult or more diagnostic detail is needed (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Management of urinary fistula
document_sections.content: General recommendations: report fistula-closure rates separately from postoperative UI rates and state the follow-up time (Strong); do not routinely place ureteric stents to prevent injury during routine gynaecological surgery (Strong); suspect ureteric injury or fistula after pelvic surgery when postoperative fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation occurs, or drainage fluid has high creatinine (Strong); use three-dimensional imaging to diagnose and locate fistulae, especially after negative direct inspection or cystoscopy (Weak); initially treat upper-tract fistulae conservatively or endoluminally where appropriate expertise and facilities exist (Weak). Surgical-principle recommendations: fistula surgeons should have sufficient training, skills and experience to choose procedures appropriately (Weak); address skin care, nutrition, rehabilitation, counselling and support before and after repair as appropriate (Weak); individualize repair timing once oedema, inflammation, tissue necrosis or infection has resolved (Weak); drain the bladder continuously until healing is verified—expert opinion suggests ten to fourteen days for simple and/or postsurgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae (Weak); avoid irradiated tissue for repair when urinary and/or faecal diversion is needed (Weak); use an interposition graft for radiation-associated fistula repair (Weak); repair persistent urogenital fistulas abdominally by open, laparoscopic or robotic means according to availability and competence (Weak); preferentially repair urethro-vaginal fistulae vaginally (Weak).

document_sections.heading: Urethral diverticulum
document_sections.content: A female urethral diverticulum is a sac-like extension made from the full urethral wall or only its mucosa, lying between peri-urethral tissue and the anterior vaginal wall.

document_sections.heading: Classification*
document_sections.content: The Limited LNS C3 classification of urethral diverticula table describes localisation as Mid-urethral, Distal, Proximal or Full length; configuration as Single, Multiloculated or Saddle shaped; communication as Mid-urethral, No communication visualised, Distal or Proximal; and continence status as Stress urinary incontinence, Continent, Post-void dribble or Mixed incontinence.

document_sections.heading: Management of urethral diverticulum
document_sections.content: Recommendations: use magnetic resonance imaging to diagnose and characterize urethral diverticula, supplementing it with urethroscopy, voiding cystourethrogram or ultrasound when needed (Weak); offer removal of symptomatic diverticula (Weak); if choosing conservative treatment, explain the small (1–6%) risk of cancer within the diverticulum (Weak); carefully assess for concurrent voiding dysfunction and UI (Strong); after appropriate counselling, treat bothersome SUI at diverticulectomy with a simultaneous non-synthetic sling (Weak); warn that new or persistent LUTS, including UI, may occur despite technically successful diverticulectomy (Strong).
